title: The Pretty Dragoon: from a Dublin Inn to the Chelsea Pension Roll
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Farm at Leixlip and the House in Dublin

stops.name: Leixlip, the farm on the Liffey
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the 1667 birth year and the Leixlip farm rest entirely on the posthumous 1740 Life, and no baptismal or parish record has been located. Tertiary summaries repeat 1667 as settled fact without noting where it comes from. Month and day are unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: Christian Cavenaugh is born to a Protestant brewer and maltster who leases a farm outside Dublin, on the Liffey at Leixlip. The house runs on two trades at once: her father's malt and his business in the city, her mother's land at the river. The girl is put to plough, rake, flail and pitchfork, and takes to them. No parish register records her name. No lease survives with her father's on it. The year, the farm and the parents themselves all come out of a book printed after she was dead.
suggested_refs: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, Commonly Call'd Mother Ross (London, 1740), pt. 1
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' Dictionary of National Biography vol. 14 (1888), via Wikisource
The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 1
Wikipedia, 'Christian Davies'

stops.name: Leixlip, too much mercury for a sedentary life
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the childhood scene and its wording come from the 1740 Life alone, whose relation to Cavanagh's own speech is unestablished. The date orders the segment and is not attested.
stops.campa: Set to needlework as a girl of her father's standing should be, she will not stay at it. She rides, she carries, she works the yard alongside the men her father hires, and she says so afterward without apology: the inclinations were always masculine, and she offers this not as a boast but as evidence. The memoir that carries the sentence is the only witness to it. Whether a woman of seventy dictated it at Chelsea or a bookseller's hack composed it in her voice cannot be settled from anything that survives.
stops.quote: I had too much mercury in me to like a sedentary life
stops.quote_source: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. John Fortescue, Soldiers' Tales (London: Peter Davies, 1928), pt. 1
suggested_refs: The companion sentence in the same passage: 'I mention this, not as worth notice, but only to show my inclinations, while a girl, were always masculine.'
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928), archive.org lifeadventuresof0000dani_t8p2

stops.name: Dublin, sent to the aunt's inn
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the DNB of 1888 repeats the episode from the 1740 Life and cites no independent record. The date is arithmetic from a birth year that is itself memoir-derived. Month and day unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: At seventeen she is seduced by her cousin Thomas Howell and, in consequence, sent off the farm to an aunt who keeps a public house in Dublin. The Victorian dictionary that repeats the story keeps a detail the popular tellers drop: Howell became a clergyman, and twenty-five years later, confronted by the woman he had ruined, killed himself. Neither the seduction nor the suicide appears in any record independent of the memoir. She is not said to have chosen the tavern. She is sent to it.
suggested_refs: The aunt's public house, unlocated: no street or sign is named in any source consulted
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888), via Wikisource
The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 1

stops.name: Dublin, the inn inherited and the waiter married
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the DNB's own arithmetic gives about 1688 but no marriage record has been located. The number of children is a memoir detail the DNB does not carry: it says only that she left her business and children with friends.
stops.campa: Four years on the aunt dies and leaves her everything. Cavanagh keeps the house running in her own name and marries Richard Welsh, a waiter in her own employment, who promises she will remain as much mistress of her effects married as single. The order matters and is usually reversed in the telling: she does not marry into the trade, she owns the trade and marries her servant. No will, no marriage entry, no address for the house has been found. Children follow, an unnumbered few, and nothing at all is known of what became of them.
stops.quote: I don't love flattery; and I know too well the character of your sex, to believe a word any one of you utter
stops.quote_source: Cavanagh's rebuff of Richard Welsh's courtship, The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928), pt. 1
suggested_refs: The aunt's will and the marriage entry, both sought and not found in any source consulted
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888), via Wikisource
The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928)

stops.name: Leixlip, the father's leave-taking after the Boyne
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the scene and the verse belong to the 1740 Life alone. The place is [R]: the memoir says only 'our house', and it distinguishes the father's business in Dublin from the mother's farm at Leixlip without saying which he rode to. The Boyne was fought 1 July 1690.
stops.campa: King James's army breaks at the Boyne and her father, who fought for it, rides home in the company of a young Frenchman to a house he cannot stay in. At three in the morning, fearing pursuit, he takes leave of his wife and children a second time, weeping, and blesses them with a verse out of Job. He dies afterward of a campaign fever. The memoir names no town for this house, only ours; his business lay in the city and her mother's land lay at Leixlip, and which of the two he came to it never says.
stops.quote: The Lord giveth, and the Lord taketh away, blessed be the name of the Lord.
stops.quote_source: Words attributed to Cavanagh's father on leaving after the Boyne, The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928), pt. 1; the line is Job 1:21
suggested_refs: Job 1:21, the scriptural commonplace the memoir puts in the father's mouth
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928), archive.org lifeadventuresof0000dani_t8p2
A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)

stops.name: Dublin, Richard Welsh does not come back
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the DNB's arithmetic puts the disappearance about 1692, four years after the marriage. Popular summaries give 1691, which contradicts the source they cite. Month and day unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: Welsh goes out on an errand of business and does not return. Nobody in Dublin can say where he went. She keeps the house, keeps the children, and hears nothing for twelve months. The accounts of what happened to him do not agree even among themselves: pressed, tricked while drunk, enlisted of his own will. The DNB says only that he mysteriously disappeared, which is the honest form of the sentence. For a year she is a woman running an inn whose husband has walked out of the record entirely.
suggested_refs: The DNB's phrase 'Welsh mysteriously disappeared', the whole of what the record supports
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888), via Wikisource
The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 1

stops.name: Dublin, the letter from Flanders
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the letter is described in the DNB and its contents dramatised in the 1740 Life. No original survives. The quoted words are Welsh's as reported by her narrative, not Cavanagh's own. Month and day unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: After twelve months a letter comes. Welsh writes that he was carried off aboard a troop ship and forced into the army in Flanders, and the memoir gives his waking aboard her in his own voice. It is the first word of him in a year and it settles nothing about how he came to be there. She now knows a country and a war. She does not know a regiment, a company, or whether the man who wrote is still alive by the time she reads it, and the letter itself does not survive; only the memoir's account of it does.
stops.quote: It is impossible for me to paint the despair I was in, finding myself thus divided from my dear wife and children
stops.quote_source: Richard Welsh's reported words on waking aboard a troop ship, The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928), pt. 1
suggested_refs: Helvoetsluys, the Dutch port the memoir names as where Welsh woke; his stop, not hers
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928)
A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)

segments.name: Christopher Welsh, Foot Soldier and Dragoon

stops.name: Dublin, the suit of his clothes
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Fortescue's introduction to the 1740 Life dates the decision to 1693, which is tighter than the 'about 1692 or 1693' of the popular accounts. No independent record of the departure exists. The pin is the standard Dublin city-centre coordinate; the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: She puts the children with kin, cuts her hair, and takes down her husband's clothes. They are the same size; the suit fits without alteration, and the memoir records that as though it were the whole argument. What she is about to do has no legal form and no procedure behind it. There is no way for a woman in 1693 to cross to Flanders and look for a soldier except to become one. The memoir gives her a single sentence of reasoning, and then she is out of the house.
stops.quote: resolved in one of his suits, for we were both of a size, to conceal my sex, and go directly for Flanders
stops.quote_source: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928), pt. 1; quoted verbatim, without the introductory 'I' that later summaries insert
suggested_refs: Fraser Easton, 'Plebeianizing the Female Soldier,' Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020)
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928), archive.org lifeadventuresof0000dani_t8p2

stops.name: Dublin, the Sign of the Golden Last
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the recruiting officer's name and the tavern sign come from the 1740 Life alone, and the house has never been located. No muster roll bearing the name Christopher Welsh has been found. The pin is the city, not the door; the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: At a Dublin house that the memoir names the Golden Last she finds Ensign Herbert Laurence beating up for recruits, and gives him the name Christopher Welsh. The zeal she professes for King William is the correct thing to say to a recruiting officer and she says it correctly. Her father had ridden home beaten from the Boyne three years earlier, fighting for the other man. She takes the enlistment money and is put on the strength of a company of foot.
stops.quote: I offered him my service to go against the French, being desirous to show my zeal for his majesty King William, and my country
stops.quote_source: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928), pt. 1
suggested_refs: Captain Tichborne's company of foot, the unit the DNB names for her first enlistment
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928)
A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)

stops.name: Landen, the skirmish before the battle
stops.date_confidence: attested for the action itself: the battle of Landen, also called Neerwinden, was fought 29 July 1693. Her presence and her wound are [R], from the 1740 Life and the DNB, and the DNB places the wound in a skirmish before the battle rather than in it. The stop is dated to the battle only to fix it in the year.
stops.campa: Her first wound comes in a skirmish, in the country before Landen, ahead of the slaughter that gives the place its name in the histories. She keeps the disguise through the surgeon's hands. The DNB says a skirmish before the battle of Landen and stops there: no limb, no side, no severity. Modern retellings hand her a leg wound at the battle itself, and neither the leg nor the battle is in the source they cite. She is treated and goes back into the ranks. Which part of her was hit, and how badly, no source consulted will say.
suggested_refs: The DNB's exact sentence: 'In a skirmish before the battle of Landen Christian received her first wound.'
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888), via Wikisource
The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 1

stops.name: Namur, taken by the French and exchanged
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The captivity and exchange are [R], from the DNB and the 1740 Life. The place is genuinely unknown: no fortress, town, month or officer is named in any source consulted. The Namur citadel pin is an explicit stand-in, chosen because the French held that fortress from 1692 to 1695, and is not attestation. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Somewhere in the Low Countries she is taken prisoner by the French, held, and exchanged, and the disguise holds through all of it. The record gives no fortress, no town, no month, and no name for the officer who exchanged her. The citadel of Namur stands in as a pin because the French held it from 1692 to 1695 and it is the likeliest place in the theatre to have kept her; it is a guess with a reason attached, not a location. A woman held among prisoners of war and not detected there: for how many weeks, and in whose keeping, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The French-held Namur citadel, 1692-1695, offered here only as a stand-in coordinate
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888), via Wikisource

stops.name: Brussels, into the dragoons
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the sources conflict openly. The DNB puts the transfer immediately after the 1694 exchange; the Royal Regiment of Scotland's learning hub gives 1697. Almack's regimental history makes Lord John Hay's colonelcy date only from 1704 and the number Second Dragoons only from 1713, so both datings carry anachronisms. The conflict is left standing. The place is unrecorded and the Brussels pin is a theatre-centre placeholder.
stops.campa: Discharged from the foot, she asks for and gets a place in the dragoons, the regiment the next century will call the Scots Greys. The sources cannot agree when. The DNB puts the transfer straight after the exchange, in 1694; the regiment's own museum says 1697; and both stumble over Lord John Hay, who did not buy the colonelcy until 1704, and over the number Second Dragoons, which the regiment did not carry until 1713. Every retelling that puts her under Hay in the 1690s is naming a commander not yet appointed.
suggested_refs: Edward Almack, The History of the Second Dragoons, 'Royal Scots Greys', on the 1704 colonelcy and the 1713 numbering
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)
Royal Regiment of Scotland Learning Hub, 'Christian (Kit) Cavanagh'
Edward Almack, regimental history of the Scots Greys (gutenberg.org/ebooks/49488)

stops.name: Rijswijk, Huis ter Nieuburch and the peace
stops.date_confidence: attested for the treaty: the Peace of Ryswick was signed at Huis ter Nieuburch in September 1697. Her discharge under it is [R], from the 1740 Life and the DNB.
stops.campa: In the house at Nieuburch outside The Hague the plenipotentiaries sign the peace, and the war she enlisted for ends. The army is broken up and the regiments sent home. Christopher Welsh is discharged with the rest: four years in the ranks, one wound, one captivity, and no husband found. The treaty is documented to the day and to the room it was signed in. Her discharge under it is documented nowhere, and for that, and for everything she does next, the memoir is the only account there is.
suggested_refs: Huis ter Nieuburch, Rijswijk, where the Nine Years' War was closed in September 1697
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)
The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 1

stops.name: Dublin, home in men's clothes
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the incognito return is a memoir claim, and the four years that follow it are undocumented in every source consulted. The month orders the segment and is not attested.
stops.campa: She comes back to Dublin in a man's coat and does not take it off. The memoir has her satisfy herself that the children are alive and cared for, and then say nothing, because she owes their keeper more than she can pay. What she lived on through the next four years, and what became of the inn she had inherited, no source consulted can say. Four years pass here with nothing in them that anybody wrote down. A woman in the city who is a man in the street, waiting for the war to start again.
suggested_refs: The Dublin inn, unrecovered and untraced through the whole interval 1697-1701
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 1
A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)

segments.name: The Meuse and the Rhine: the War Renewed

stops.name: The Hague, back to Holland and re-enlisted
stops.date_confidence: attested for the war: hostilities over the Spanish succession resumed in 1701. Her re-enlistment is [R], dated to 1701 by both the DNB and the Royal Regiment of Scotland; the secondary summaries giving 1702 contradict the source they cite. The pin is a placeholder, since no landing place or town is recorded. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The Spanish succession puts Europe back under arms, and she crosses again and re-enlists, this time in the dragoons. The DNB dates it 1701; the regimental museum agrees; the popular accounts that say 1702 are a year adrift of their own footnotes. She is thirty-four and goes back to a trade she has not practised in four years. Where in Holland she came ashore and signed is not recorded anywhere, and the pin marks the seat of the States General rather than any place she is known to have stood.
suggested_refs: The DNB's sentence: 'On the renewal of the war in 1701 she went back to Holland and re-enlisted with Lord John Hay.'
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)
Royal Regiment of Scotland Learning Hub, 'Christian (Kit) Cavanagh'

stops.name: Venlo, Fort St Michael carried
stops.date_confidence: attested for the siege: Venlo fell to the allies in September 1702, and the regimental account places the Greys covering the sieges of Venloo, Ruremonde and Stevenswaert. Her individual presence is [R], from the 1740 Life.
stops.campa: The allied army works its way up the Meuse and Fort St Michael is carried, first of the season's forts. Her regiment covers the siege. The memoir takes her through it in the plural, with the army, in passages that read like a campaign history rather than a life. That is the difficulty with the middle of the book: the itinerary is real and independently attested, and her name is nowhere in it except where she puts it herself. Ruremonde and Stevenswaert fall in the same weeks. Her regiment covers those sieges too.
suggested_refs: The regimental account of the Scots Greys 'covering the sieges of Venloo, Ruremonde and Stevenswaert' (gutenberg.org/ebooks/49488)
sources: Edward Almack, regimental history of the Scots Greys (gutenberg.org/ebooks/49488)
The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2

stops.name: Liege, the citadel stormed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the operation: the citadel of Liege was stormed in October 1702. Her presence is [R], from the 1740 Life alone.
stops.campa: Marlborough turns on Liege and takes the citadel by storm in October, closing his first year in command with the Meuse open from Maastricht downward. The dragoons are in the field for it. The memoir puts her there in the same voice it uses for everything else it did not witness, and the reader is left to work out how much of an army a single trooper actually sees. She is thirty-five years old and nine years in uniform, counting the four years of the first war.
suggested_refs: The citadel of Liege, taken by storm in October 1702
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2
Edward Almack, regimental history of the Scots Greys

stops.name: Bonn, the siege on the Rhine
stops.date_confidence: attested for the siege: Bonn capitulated in May 1703. Her presence is [R], from the 1740 Life alone; no pay list, wound or anecdote fixes her there in particular.
stops.campa: The army moves off the Meuse to the Rhine and invests Bonn, the elector's residence. It surrenders in May after a fortnight under the guns. The campaign narrative carries her along with it. No pay list, no wound and no anecdote fixes her at Bonn in particular; the town is in her story because her regiment's year passed through it. Bonn is the last of the northern sieges, and the last place on the Rhine she is said to have stood. The following spring the army marches south.
suggested_refs: The electoral residence at Bonn, invested and taken in May 1703
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2

stops.name: Huy, the citadel on the Meuse
stops.date_confidence: attested for the siege: Huy was taken in August 1703. Her presence is [R], from the 1740 Life alone.
stops.campa: Back on the Meuse the allies take Huy in August, a fortress standing on a rock over the river. The memoir keeps her with the army through it and records nothing that happened to her there. The French will retake the place and lose it again before the peace, and she will be nowhere near it either time. This is the last of the low-country stops that can be listed without a wound attached to her body. From here the campaign turns south and east, toward the Danube.
suggested_refs: The citadel of Huy, taken August 1703
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2

stops.name: Schellenberg, the ball that stayed in
stops.date_confidence: attested for the action: the entrenchments on the Schellenberg above Donauworth were stormed on 2 July 1704. The hip wound and the unextracted ball are [R], from the 1740 Life; the 1717 War Office order attests only 'divers Wounds' in general, without count or location.
stops.campa: The army has marched from the Meuse to the Danube in six weeks and storms the entrenched heights above Donauworth on a July evening at heavy cost. A musket ball goes into her hip and stays there. The memoir says it was never cut out and that she carried it for the rest of her life, which is thirty-five years of walking with lead in the hip. The War Office papers that will one day pay her a pension speak only of divers Wounds, without a count and without a location.
suggested_refs: The regimental account of 'the lofty heights of Schellenberg' (gutenberg.org/ebooks/49488)
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2
Edward Almack, regimental history of the Scots Greys
TNA WO 4/20 fo. 182, quoted in Fraser Easton, Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020)

stops.name: Blindheim, the guard over the prisoners
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle: Blenheim was fought 13 August 1704, and Almack gives the date. The reunion is [R], from the 1740 Life and repeated by the DNB. Whether Welsh stood among the guard or among the guarded is not stated by either source, and the file does not resolve it.
stops.campa: Six weeks later the French and Bavarian army is destroyed in the Danube valley and thousands of prisoners are taken. She is set as one of the guard over a body of them, and there, after thirteen years, she sees Richard Welsh. The DNB says exactly that much: forming one of a guard to some prisoners, she again saw her husband. It does not say he was one of the prisoners. The popular versions that make him a captive of the guard she was standing in have supplied that themselves.
suggested_refs: The DNB's sentence: 'While forming one of a guard to some prisoners taken in that battle she again saw her husband, after a separation of thirteen years.'
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)
Edward Almack, regimental history of the Scots Greys
The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2

stops.name: Blindheim, the husband made a brother
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the arrangement by which Welsh passed as her brother is a memoir claim with no independent support. The stop is dated to the day after the battle only to order the segment.
stops.campa: Having found him, she does not resume the marriage. The memoir has her pass Welsh off as her brother so that Christopher Welsh may go on being a dragoon, and has him agree to it. Thirteen years of searching end in an arrangement that keeps the disguise the search was conducted in. What the two of them actually said to each other in the Bavarian camp is known only from a book printed thirty-six years later. How the thing was put to him, and what he said back, nobody else ever wrote down.
suggested_refs: Richard Welsh, private in a foot regiment; Almack names no unit beyond 'a foot regiment'
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2
A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)

stops.name: Ramillies, the shell from the steeple
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle: Ramillies was fought 23 May 1706. The head wound is [R], from the 1740 Life, repeated by the DNB and by the regiment's own museum; no official record documents it.
stops.campa: The French line is broken in an afternoon on the plateau between the Mehaigne and the Gette. A shell fired from a church steeple in the village comes down on the back of her head, and the skull is fractured. She has been thirteen years in the ranks by now: wounded in the country before Landen, wounded on the Schellenberg, taken prisoner by the French and exchanged, and never once examined. This is the wound that ends the career. It is the one that puts her under the surgeons' hands with her hat off.
stops.quote: when an unlucky shell from a steeple, on which, before the battle, they had planted some mortars and cannon, which played all the time of the engagement, struck the back part of my head and fractured my skull
stops.quote_source: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928), pt. 2
suggested_refs: Almack's chapter heading calling her 'a famous Amazon, wounded as a trooper of the Greys at Ramillies'
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928), archive.org lifeadventuresof0000dani_t8p2
A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)
Royal Regiment of Scotland Learning Hub, 'Christian (Kit) Cavanagh'

stops.name: Ramillies, what they told Brigadier Preston
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the discovery scene belongs to the 1740 Life and no official record attests it. The stop is dated the day after the battle to order the segment. The DNB says dismissal from the service followed and Almack says she had to cease to be a trooper; the claim found in some retellings that Lord John Hay intervened to keep her with the army has no source at all.
stops.campa: The surgeons open her clothes to work on the head and find what thirteen years of soldiers, officers, surgeons and prisoners had not found. They report it upward. The regiment had called her the pretty dragoon, a joke that was not a joke, and the name goes to the brigadier attached to the discovery. Dismissal from the service follows. The DNB says it followed naturally, as though nothing else were available, and by the law and custom of the time nothing else was.
stops.quote: No sooner had they made this discovery, but they acquainted Brigadier Preston, that his pretty dragoon (so I was always called) was, in fact, a woman.
stops.quote_source: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928), pt. 2
suggested_refs: The intervening passage in the memoir, in which the surgeons conclude from her body that she had borne children
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies, ed. Fortescue (1928)
A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)
Edward Almack, regimental history of the Scots Greys

stops.name: Aughrim, the other account
stops.date_confidence: contested. The battle of Aughrim was fought 12 July 1691 and the stop is dated to it. Boyer's obituary of July 1739 places her exposure here, in the Inniskilling Regiment; the 1740 Life and the DNB place it at Ramillies in 1706 in the North British Dragoons. The surviving War Office orders of 1717 and 1720 name the North British Dragoons and the wars in Flanders, which favours the Ramillies line, but they say nothing about where or when she was discovered. The contradiction is unresolved here.
stops.campa: There is a second story, and it is not late invention. In the month she died, Abel Boyer printed in the Political State of Great Britain that Christiana Davies had served several years undiscovered as a dragoon in the Royal Inniskilling Regiment, and was found out on taking a wound at Aughrim in Ireland, in King William's war. Not Ramillies, not Flanders, not the Greys. The DNB set the two accounts side by side in 1888 and declined to choose between them.
stops.quote: Died at Chelsea, Mrs. Christiana Davies, who for several years served as a dragoon undiscovered in the Royal Inniskillen Regiment, but receiving a wound in King William's wars at Aughrim in Ireland, was discovered.
stops.quote_source: Abel Boyer, The Political State of Great Britain lviii. 90 (1739), quoted in A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' Dictionary of National Biography vol. 14 (1888)
suggested_refs: Abel Boyer, The Political State of Great Britain lviii. 90; the DNB also has her father present at the Boyne and at Aughrim, dying afterward of campaign fever
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888), via Wikisource
TNA WO 4/20 and WO 4/23, via Fraser Easton, Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020)

segments.name: The Sutler's Trade: Oudenarde to Bouchain

stops.name: Oudenarde, water to the mouth of a cannon
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle: Oudenarde was fought 11 July 1708. Her presence is [R], from the 1740 Life; the quoted death notice attests the trade in general and names no battle.
stops.campa: She stays with the army now in women's clothes, cooking, selling, foraging, carrying water. At Oudenarde the allies catch the French crossing the Scheldt and beat them in a fight fed in piecemeal until dark. The press notice printed the week she died says plainly what she was worth on such a day: useful in a battle or a siege, supplying the soldiers with water and other necessaries, even to the mouth of a cannon. The notice names no battle at all.
stops.quote: was very useful in a Battle or a Siege to supply the Soldiers, &c. with Water and other Necessaries, even to the Mouth of a Cannon
stops.quote_source: Daily Post, 10 July 1739, quoted in Fraser Easton, 'Plebeianizing the Female Soldier,' Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020)
suggested_refs: The London death notices of July 1739, independent of the 1740 memoir
sources: Fraser Easton, 'Plebeianizing the Female Soldier,' Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020)
The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2

stops.name: Lille, four months in the lines
stops.date_confidence: attested for the siege: the town of Lille fell in October and its citadel in December 1708. Her presence is [R], memoir only. The month orders the stop within the siege.
stops.campa: Vauban's masterwork holds out from August into December, the town first and then the citadel, the longest and costliest siege of the war. The Greys are in the covering force. A sutler's season in the lines at Lille means four months of mud, sickness and rising prices, which is the part of a siege that pays a sutler and kills a soldier. Her presence there rests on the memoir, and the memoir keeps her there because it keeps her with the regiment throughout.
suggested_refs: The citadel of Lille, Vauban's own work, surrendered December 1708
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2

stops.name: Tournai, the war under the ground
stops.date_confidence: attested for the siege: Tournai was invested in June 1709 and its citadel surrendered in September. Her presence is [R], memoir only.
stops.campa: The 1709 campaign opens against Tournai, a siege fought as much underground as above it, mine against countermine in chalk galleries beneath the glacis. It takes until September to finish the citadel. The army that walks away from it walks to Malplaquet eight days later. She is with it, by her own account, selling to the men who dug. Nothing outside the memoir puts her name in the trenches at Tournai; the regiment's itinerary is what puts her there.
suggested_refs: The mine and countermine galleries beneath the citadel of Tournai, 1709
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2

stops.name: Malplaquet, the day of the battle
stops.date_confidence: attested for the battle: Malplaquet was fought 11 September 1709, and Almack gives the date. Richard Welsh's death in it is [R], from the 1740 Life and the DNB, and is not tied to any casualty return.
stops.campa: In the woods and the gap between them the allies force the French position and pay for it with a loss reckoned in the tens of thousands, the worst day of the war and the worst in Europe for a century after. Richard Welsh is killed in it, in the foot regiment nobody has ever named. She does not learn this in the evening; she learns it the next morning, out on the ground. The field is a mile and more of hedge, wood and standing corn, and the dead lie in it where the lines stood.
suggested_refs: The field of Malplaquet, near Taisnieres-sur-Hon, 11 September 1709
sources: Edward Almack, regimental history of the Scots Greys
A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)
The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2

stops.name: Malplaquet, the morning after
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the search of the field, the figure of two hundred bodies and the Captain Ross etymology all come from the 1740 Life and from the DNB's report of what 'it is said'. No Captain Ross has been identified in any record. A 1734 press notice is sometimes cited as showing the surname in circulation before the memoir; that notice could not be located in this research and is not relied on.
stops.campa: She goes out over the field turning bodies until she finds him, and buries him where he lies. Two hundred turned over is the memoir's figure and nobody has ever audited it. What the DNB records is not the number but the noise she made, and an officer named Ross who was moved by it, and from whom the name is said to come. She had been the pretty dragoon. She is Mother Ross from this morning onward, on the strength of a sentence that says it is said. The captain has never been identified.
stops.quote: her lamentations at the discovery were so extravagant as to excite the open commiseration of a captain Ross, whence, it is said, she gained the sobriquet of Mother Ross
stops.quote_source: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' Dictionary of National Biography vol. 14 (1888), via Wikisource
suggested_refs: The Royal Regiment of Scotland's account, which repeats the figure of two hundred bodies turned over
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)

stops.name: Douai, the first of four fortresses
stops.date_confidence: attested for the siege: Douai capitulated in June 1710. Her presence is [R], memoir only.
stops.campa: The next year's campaign is a siege war along the Scarpe and the Lys, four fortresses in seven months, and she goes with it as she has gone with everything since Ramillies: with a pack, a stock of drink, and no rank. Douai falls in June after two months of open trenches. There is nothing personal in the record of it. The place is on her itinerary because it was on her regiment's, and the memoir folds the whole sequence into her account without distinguishing what she saw from what the army did.
suggested_refs: The 1710 siege sequence: Douai, Bethune, Saint-Venant, Aire
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2

stops.name: Bethune, a blank summer
stops.date_confidence: attested for the siege: Bethune fell at the end of August 1710, and Almack's regimental history places the Greys in the sequence. Her presence is [R], memoir only.
stops.campa: Bethune is opened at the end of August after a month of trenches, and the army moves on within days. Almack's regimental history gives the order plainly: after Bethune fell they were occupied with the sieges of Aire and Saint-Venant. The Greys are in the covering force. She is behind them with the rest of the followers, and the record of her personally is blank for the whole of this summer. A sutler's presence at a siege leaves no paper unless she is robbed, tried, or paid.
suggested_refs: Almack: after Bethune fell, 'they were occupied with the sieges of Aire and Saint-Venant'
sources: Edward Almack, regimental history of the Scots Greys (gutenberg.org/ebooks/49488)
The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2

stops.name: Saint-Venant, the second husband dies
stops.date_confidence: attested for the siege: Saint-Venant was taken at the end of September 1710. The marriage to Hugh Jones and his death wound are [R]. The DNB dates the marriage to within three months of September 1709; the Royal Regiment of Scotland dates it to 1710, the same year as the death. The conflict is left standing.
stops.campa: Within about three months of Welsh's death she had married again, a grenadier named Hugh Jones. At Saint-Venant, a small place on the Lys taken at the end of September, Jones takes the wound that kills him. The sources cannot even agree when the marriage was: the DNB puts it inside 1709, three months after Malplaquet, and the regiment's own museum puts it in 1710, the year he died. No service record for Jones has been found, and no burial entry either.
suggested_refs: Hugh Jones, grenadier; no service or casualty record located under that name
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)

stops.name: Bouchain, the last siege of the war
stops.date_confidence: attested for the siege: Bouchain fell in September 1711. Her presence is [R], memoir only.
stops.campa: Marlborough passes the lines the French had named ne plus ultra and takes Bouchain in September. It is the last place he takes: he is recalled to London before the year is out, and the war closes without him. She is twice widowed and forty-four years old, with a ball in her hip and a fractured skull healed over. Eighteen years of her life have gone into the train of an army, most of them in a coat cut for a man. Ahead of her is a country she has not properly lived in since she was twenty-five.
suggested_refs: The lines of Ne Plus Ultra, passed in August 1711 before the siege of Bouchain
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2
Edward Almack, regimental history of the Scots Greys

stops.name: London, the lodgings after the peace
stops.date_confidence: attested as a reading of the primary text: Fraser Easton (2020) takes the detail from the 1740 Life itself. The memoir remains [R] throughout, and the lodging is not otherwise documented; the district is unrecorded and the pin is the city. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: She comes to London to press her case for a pension. Fraser Easton, reading the Life closely in 2020, finds her lodging for a time in a brothel before the Whig officers who knew her in Flanders take up the petition on her behalf. The popular accounts and the museum pages leave that out and go straight from the war to the palace. The sanitising is not a modern habit; it is only more thorough now than it was. The district of the lodging is not recorded, and the pin is the city.
suggested_refs: Fraser Easton, 'Plebeianizing the Female Soldier,' Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020): 432
sources: Fraser Easton, 'Plebeianizing the Female Soldier,' Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020)

stops.name: St James's Palace, the audience nobody recorded
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The presentation to Queen Anne through the Duke of Argyll is [R], from the 1740 Life. The DNB gives a shilling a day and no bounty; Wikipedia and the Royal Regiment of Scotland give fifty pounds and a shilling a day. No official paper of Anne's reign has been located, and the earliest documented order is TNA WO 4/20, dated 19 July 1717. The month orders the stop.
stops.campa: Tradition brings her before Queen Anne, presented by the Duke of Argyll, who knew what she had been in the field, and has the Queen give her fifty pounds and a shilling a day for life. The fifty pounds is not in the DNB, which gives only the shilling; it comes in from later sources. The audience itself is undocumented. What is documented is that the first surviving pension order is dated five years afterward, under a different sovereign, and for five pence.
suggested_refs: John Campbell, 2nd Duke of Argyll, named by the memoir as her advocate at court
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)
Royal Regiment of Scotland Learning Hub, 'Christian (Kit) Cavanagh'

stops.name: Dublin, the tavern not recovered
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the failed property claim, the beer and pie shop and the third marriage all come from the 1740 Life and later summaries. Davies's given name is unestablished, and the Dictionary of Irish Biography's characterisation of him could not be checked directly in this research. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Twenty years after she walked out of it in her husband's suit she comes back to Dublin to claim the house her aunt had left her, and cannot get it. Too long gone, no papers, no witnesses left who count. She opens a beer and pie shop instead, and marries a soldier named Davies, whose given name nobody has established and whom the biographical tradition remembers chiefly for drinking what they earned. She takes his name, and it is the name the London papers will print when she dies.
suggested_refs: Dictionary of Irish Biography, 'Davies, Christian', on the third husband
sources: The Life and Adventures of Mrs. Christian Davies (1740), pt. 2

stops.name: Royal Hospital Chelsea, five pence a day
stops.date_confidence: attested. TNA Discovery confirms WO 4/20 as the Secretary-at-War's general out-letters covering April to December 1717, which brackets 19 July 1717. The wording is quoted from Easton (2020), who worked from the document; the original was not fetched in this research. Easton's note gives 'fo. 182'.
stops.campa: The Secretary at War writes to the Chelsea commissioners and orders five pence a day paid for her future support and maintenance. It is the earliest document of her life that is neither memoir nor obituary, an out-letter in a numbered War Office volume, signed by James Craggs in July 1717. The regiment, the theatre, the disguise and the wounds are all conceded in it, in a clerk's abbreviations. Five pence a day was the rate for an ordinary broken private.
stops.quote: she serv'd sevl. Years in the late Warr in Flanders in the Royll. Regt. of North British Drags. ... disguis'd in the habit of a man ... suffer'd very much by divers Wounds she receiv'd in follg. the said Regt.
stops.quote_source: Secretary-at-War James Craggs to the Commissioners of Chelsea Hospital, 19 July 1717, TNA WO 4/20 fo. 182, quoted as three separate fragments in Fraser Easton, 'Plebeianizing the Female Soldier,' Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020), 434; ellipses mark Easton's own connecting words, which are not in the document's quoted text
suggested_refs: TNA WO 4/20, War Office Secretary-at-War out-letters, April to December 1717
sources: Fraser Easton, 'Plebeianizing the Female Soldier,' Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020), 434
The National Archives Discovery catalogue, WO 4/20

stops.name: Royal Hospital Chelsea, the admission book
stops.date_confidence: attested; the entry is quoted verbatim from TNA WO 116/1 by Easton (2020), who transcribes it directly from the register. The original was not fetched in this research, and the orthography of 'fatt jolly' varies slightly between modern citations.
stops.campa: In November she is examined in person and written into the hospital's admission book under the name Welsh, serving in what the clerk calls the Stairs Dragoons. He looks at her and puts down what he sees: a fatt jolly woman who received several wounds in the service in the habit of a man. The wording is the hand he uses for every applicant, and nothing in it is impressed by her. She is fifty years old by the memoir's arithmetic, and she is on the out-pension list.
stops.quote: a fatt jolly woman [who] received Several wounds in the Service in ye habitt of a man
stops.quote_source: Royal Hospital Chelsea admission book, 19 November 1717, TNA WO 116/1, quoted in Fraser Easton, 'Plebeianizing the Female Soldier,' Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020), 433
suggested_refs: TNA WO 116/1, Royal Hospital Chelsea admission book
sources: Fraser Easton, 'Plebeianizing the Female Soldier,' Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020), 433

stops.name: Royal Hospital Chelsea, notwithstanding her being a woman
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the order and its wording, quoted from Easton (2020) and cited as TNA WO 4/23 fo. 17. The document itself was not independently fetched or imaged in this research, so the shelfmark rests on Easton's citation and on the dossier's parallel reference.
stops.campa: Three years on, a second Secretary at War more than doubles it: one shilling a day, the rate of an ordinary Chelsea out-pensioner. The clause that carries the increase is the interesting part. Notwithstanding her being a woman, she served many years very faithfully in the late wars in Flanders. The state has no category for what she did, so it writes one on the spot, as a concession, inside a subordinate clause. The shilling is the same figure tradition had assigned to Queen Anne eight years earlier.
stops.quote: notwithstanding her being a Woman, [she] serv'd many years very faithfully in the late Wars in Flanders
stops.quote_source: Secretary-at-War George Treby, 7 July 1720, TNA WO 4/23 fo. 17, quoted in Fraser Easton, 'Plebeianizing the Female Soldier,' Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020)

stops.name: London, the name already in print
stops.date_confidence: unverified lead. A 1734 political satire is cited in secondary summaries of Easton's archival work as naming a famous female dragoon called Sarah Ross on a government pension. The notice could not be located or read in this research; the publication is given variously as The Craftsman and as the Gentleman's Magazine. The pin is the London print district generally, not an address, and the month orders the stop.
stops.campa: A political satire published in London is said to have named a famous female dragoon, Sarah Ross, who served in men's clothes and drew a government pension. If the notice exists it proves the name was in public circulation five years before she died and six before the book that made her famous. It could not be located in this research: not in the Craftsman, not in the Gentleman's Magazine, not anywhere reachable. The lead is set down here because it is checkable, not because it has been checked.
suggested_refs: The 1734 notice, variously attributed to The Craftsman and the Gentleman's Magazine; unlocated
sources: Fraser Easton, 'Plebeianizing the Female Soldier,' Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020), cited at second hand for this item

stops.name: Royal Hospital Chelsea, taken from her own mouth
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the dictation is claimed by the 1740 title page and by nothing else, and the stop is dated to her last full year only to order the segment. The DNB rejected the Defoe attribution in 1888 as resting on no reasonable grounds; the Fortescue reprint of 1928 still carried Defoe's name. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: The title page of the book that will carry her name for three centuries says it was taken from her own mouth when a pensioner of Chelsea Hospital. Somebody sat with her in the last years and wrote. Who he was, and how much he invented, is the whole problem of her life. The eighteenth century assigned the book to Defoe; the DNB said in 1888 that the attribution rested on no reasonable grounds and that the thing reads more like a history of Marlborough's campaigns than a memoir. A 1928 reprint put Defoe's name on it anyway.
suggested_refs: The full 1740 title: '...who, in several campaigns under King William and the late Duke of Marlborough, in the quality of a foot-soldier and dragoon, gave many signal proofs of an unparallelled courage and personal bravery. Taken from her own mouth when a pensioner of Chelsea-Hospital.'
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)

stops.name: Royal Hospital Chelsea, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested; the death at Chelsea on 7 July 1739 is corroborated by the Daily Post of 10 July 1739, by the DNB, and by the regiment's own account. The clinical cause is [R], the feverish cold of the tradition. Her age depends on a birth year that is memoir-derived and otherwise unsupported.
stops.campa: She dies at Chelsea after a short feverish illness, caught, the accounts say, nursing the third husband through his own. She is seventy-one or seventy-two, if the birth year is right, and nothing certifies the birth year. The London papers report the death within three days, which is the strongest thing about it: the date and the place come from print set while people who had known her were alive to contradict it. Nobody printed a cause beyond the fever.
suggested_refs: Daily Post, 10 July 1739; Daily Advertiser, 10 July 1739
sources: Fraser Easton, 'Plebeianizing the Female Soldier,' Eighteenth-Century Fiction 32.3 (2020), 432 n.15

stops.name: Royal Hospital Chelsea, the Old Burial Ground
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial ground and the honours, from the DNB's summary of the death-era reports and from the Royal Hospital's own tradition; the individual grave has never been located and the exact day of burial is not recorded, so the date orders the stop only. The first admission of women as In-Pensioners in March 2009 is attested; no located Royal Hospital source invokes Cavanagh as a forerunner, and no such linkage is asserted here.
stops.campa: She is buried among the pensioners in the hospital's own ground, and volleys are fired over the grave, three of them by the usual account. The ground holds something near ten thousand people, almost all of them unmarked, and hers was never identified; the pin is the field, not a plot. In March 2009 the Royal Hospital admitted women as In-Pensioners for the first time in its history. No Royal Hospital source consulted here connects that to the woman it had already paid a shilling a day and buried among its men.
suggested_refs: The Old Burial Ground of the Royal Hospital Chelsea, roughly ten thousand largely unmarked interments, 1691-1854
sources: A. R. Vian, 'Davies, Christian,' DNB vol. 14 (1888)
